contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
contributions.text_english: Diolch, Cabinet Minister. In Blaenau Gwent, nearly three in 10 residents aged 16 and over have no formal qualifications, which is the highest proportion in the whole of Wales, while neighbouring Caerphilly has the fourth highest. I've seen first-hand the vital role that organisations such as ACT has in Ebbw Vale. They play such an important role in supporting young people facing really complex needs and barriers to education, training and employment. For many of these young people, progress can mean overcoming mental health challenges, gaining qualifications after leaving school without any, finding secure housing or even turning away from crime as well. They need to have a system that can respond to the full range of barriers they face as an individual and gives them the best opportunity as well to fulfil their potential. So, Cabinet Minister, how will the Welsh Government ensure we have a fit-for-purpose system, with the flexibility and stability needed to support young people to fulfil their potential, particularly those facing extreme barriers?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the First Minister
contributions.text_english: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Motor neurone disease, as you said, is such a devastating, rapidly progressing condition, and, for those people who are living with it, time is really critical. I lost my auntie to MND a couple of years ago, and I saw first-hand the devastating impact that that had on her and our family as well. Around a third of people who are diagnosed with MND die within a year of that diagnosis, yet the MND Association tells us that securing funding for vital home adaptation can take just as long. And that funding is about so much more than just home improvements. It's about preserving people's independence, their dignity and also their quality of life. Constituents have contacted me about the difficulties that they face in securing these adaptations. People with MND shouldn't have to spend their precious time waiting for their homes to be made safe and accessible for them. So, Prif Weinidog, what steps are the Welsh Government taking to address the critical housing challenges faced by people living with MND in Wales?

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability: Winter preparedness: Be flood ready
contributions.text_english: Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement today. Flooding remains a real worry for communities across Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni and the whole of Wales, especially as we see this much more extreme weather happening year on year. Research by the British Red Cross highlights the challenges that are faced by people in vulnerable situations when flooding eventually happens. The research found that most people were completely unprepared when flooding hit. Many were displaced for months from their homes, often living in unsuitable accommodation, struggled to get recovery grants, and almost all of them said that their mental health had been significantly impacted by the flooding. So, I was just wondering what the Welsh Government was going to do to make sure that our most vulnerable communities in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni are better prepared for flooding and get the support they need when it happens, especially that mental health support as well in the longer term.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Firstly, I would like to thank all the Members who have shown their support for this debate today. I especially want to thank Elwyn Vaughan, who has worked closely with me on this motion and has been a strong advocate for change in his constituency as well. The fact that this motion has support from Members across the Senedd and from different parts of Wales is significant, because contaminated land is not an isolated or local problem. It's a legacy of our shared industrial past, which communities across Wales live with to this day. I look forward to hearing from Members in this debate, and particularly about the experiences of communities in their own constituencies.

For many people across Wales, our industrial past is not simply something confined to the history books. It's something that communities continue to live with today. We see that with our coal tips, which remain a visible part of the landscape in many of our communities. But the legacy of contaminated land is often much harder to see. Toxic substances left behind by historic industrial activity can remain in our ground for decades after that activity has ended, and in the case of some chemicals, they can be in our ground for generations.

So, what do we mean when we talk about contaminated land? As Natural Resources Wales explains, land can become contaminated through previous industrial, commercial or landfill uses, including where contamination has migrated from an adjacent site. That can include heavy metals, such as arsenic, cadmium and lead, oils and tars, solvents and gases, alongside radioactive substances. And those consequences can extend beyond the disposal site itself, with contamination potentially affecting human health, animal health and also our wider environment. We've also heard increasing public concerns about persistent chemicals, such as polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs—a group of toxic, human-made, hazardous chemicals that have dangerous effects on our environment and our health, which can remain in the environment for long periods of time.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
contributions.text_english:
The recent BBC documentary Buried, presented by Michael Sheen, has brought renewed attention to this issue of contaminated land, which I very much welcome, and I would like to thank all of those who have been involved in its production. However, we must recognise that, for many communities, these concerns have been raised by them for many years. Campaigners and communities across Wales have been raising these issues with us, and quite a few of them are actually up there in the gallery today.

And I've seen the impact of that legacy first-hand in my own constituency. In Ynysddu, Ty Llwyd quarry was actually featured in the recent documentary, with the two Jans. It's a site where local people have been raising concerns for years about the historical disposal of chemical waste, its links to Monsanto's former manufacturing plant in Newport and what that legacy could mean for the surrounding community. There have also been concerns about leachate leaving the former quarry site, particularly following periods of heavy rainfall, and the potential for contaminants to move then into the surrounding area.

I want to take this opportunity to thank Councillor Janine Reid, who is here as well today, and also her colleague Councillor Jan Jones, for the tireless work that they have done to raise these concerns and make sure that their community's voice is heard.

But, ultimately, Ty Llwyd is about more than what is happening at a former quarry site. It's about the people who live alongside it. For those people, this is not an abstract environmental issue. It's something that's been hanging over the community for years. It's about the place where people live, where their children have grown up and where people go and walk their dogs. It's about being able to feel confident that the place they call home is safe and that their community and its future are being protected.

As Councillor Reid put it:

'For our community, Ty Llwyd is not an abstract environmental issue—it is something that has been hanging over us for years. The consequences of what has happened here are felt by the people who live alongside it.

'We need the contamination to be properly understood, the risks to our community to be taken seriously, and a clear plan to ensure that Ty Llwyd along with other sites in Wales, do not continue to be a source of concern for local people—with reassurance that our community and its future are being protected.'

And I think that quote from Janine gets to the real heart of this issue today. People shouldn't have to live for years with unanswered questions about what may be beneath their feet, what may be moving through the land around them, or what the potential risks could be. They deserve clear information about what is known, a proper understanding of the risks, and confidence that there is a clear plan in place on how we deal with those risks. And, as we know, Ty Llwyd is not unique. Across Wales, there are thousands of sites with a history of industrial or other potentially contaminating activity—from north to south, from Cefn Mawr to Maendy, communities across Wales are living alongside that legacy.

Research by Friends of the Earth Cymru has identified more than 45,000 potentially contaminated land sites across Wales. And while that gives us some indication of the scale of this issue, it also highlights the fact that we still do not have a clear national picture of potentially contaminated land across Wales. We need to know where these sites are, what contaminants may be present and which pose the greatest risks to our communities and to our environment. And that is why this motion today calls for a national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising those sites that pose the greatest risks. We need to know where these sites are. We need to understand what contamination may be present and the risks it poses. And we need to make sure that the sites presenting the greatest risks are prioritised.

But there is also another important issue here, and that is who pays. The principle of 'polluters pay' should be at the heart of this approach. Where the person or the company responsible for pollution can be identified and held responsible, they should contribute towards the costs of putting it right. That burden should not simply fall on our local authorities, and it shouldn't fall on the taxpayers either.

But. of course, as we know, with historical contamination it's not always straightforward. Some companies may no longer exist. Ownership may have changed. Records may be incomplete. That's why the motion also calls for the UK Government to introduce a dedicated funding mechanism for cases where the costs cannot be recovered, because there has to be a solution for those sites as well. We cannot have a situation where a local authority knows there is a potential problem, but does not have the resources to properly address it. And we cannot expect communities to carry the burden of historical industrial activity simply because the pollution happened many years ago.

Local authorities, Natural Resources Wales and other organisations are already doing important work in identifying, investigating and managing contaminated land. But they need the resources and the support to fulfil those responsibilities. And communities need confidence that, when they raise concerns, those concerns will be properly investigated.

So, Dirprwy Lywydd, this motion is ultimately about making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly. It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land. It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest. It's about giving local authorities the support that they need. And it's about making sure that, where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right.

The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks or the costs. For those reasons, Dirprwy Lywydd, I hope Members across the Siambr will support this motion today. Diolch yn fawr.

The recent BBC documentary Buried, presented by Michael Sheen, has brought renewed attention to this issue of contaminated land, which I very much welcome, and I would like to thank all of those who have been involved in its production. I want to take this opportunity to thank Councillor Janine Reid, who is here as well today, and also her colleague Councillor Jan Jones, for the tireless work that they have done to raise these concerns and make sure that their community's voice is heard.

But, ultimately, Ty Llwyd is about more than what is happening at a former quarry site. It's about the people who live alongside it. For those people, this is not an abstract environmental issue. It's something that's been hanging over the community for years. It's about the place where people live, where their children have grown up and where people go and walk their dogs. It's about being able to feel confident that the place they call home is safe and that their community and its future are being protected.

For some, that legacy is visible in the land around them and in the concerns they continue to raise about what may have been left behind. Contaminated land is an important part of that legacy. The substances that are left behind by historical industrial activity can pose, as we've all mentioned, real serious risks to people, to animals and the wider environment. And for communities—a lot of them sat up there in the gallery, again, today—who are living alongside these sites, that uncertainty about what is there, about what risks it may pose and what happens next can be really difficult for them to live with.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Welsh Labour Debate: Further education
contributions.text_english:
I'm glad also that we have the opportunity today to discuss NEETs, so I thank Lynne Neagle as well for bringing forward this really important debate, but also the chance to discuss why young people find themselves in this position as well. Not too long ago, I raised this issue here in the Senedd, particularly the long-term impact that being out of education, employment or training can have on a young person's chances in life. As one of the youngest Members in the Senedd—I think Ben actually might win the award just above me, just about—this is something that is really personal to me as well.

The recent Milburn report highlighted the real scale of this challenge, with around 56,000 young people in Wales. Again, that statistic's been bounced around, but that's 17 per cent of all 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training. 

Now, there are lots of reasons why a young person might find themselves in this position. It could be difficulties at school, mental health, child poverty, transport, or simply not having the right support at the right time. In the constituency that I represent, Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, we're seeing some of these challenges very clearly. Back in June, I raised this with the First Minister, pointing out that Blaenau Gwent has the highest proportion of residents aged 16 and over with no qualifications in Wales—that's 27.9 per cent—while Caerphilly is fourth among all local authorities.

Now, those figures are really concerning, but what concerns me more is what they can mean for a young person that's growing up in these communities. That's why early intervention really matters as well. We need to support young people before they reach the point of completely disengaging, and I've seen some really good examples of this in my own constituency. A couple of weeks ago, I visited ACT training in Ebbw Vale. They're supporting young people who, for all sorts of reasons, haven't found that typical conventional route from school into further education, training or employment. And I just want to put on the record as well my thanks to all of the staff there for the work that they do, because it was really inspiring, that visit. And there was one thing that really stood out to me that one of the staff said during that visit. They told me that, for some of the young people that they work with, the support that they provide can quite literally be the difference between life and death for that young person, and I think that really brings home again the real seriousness of this situation. Because we can talk about NEET rates and percentages like I did at the start, but, for that young person, this isn't a statistic. It's their life.

Further education and training have a huge role to play, but there are also wider barriers as well that can make it so hard for a young person to take that next step. If they're struggling with their mental health, they may not be in a position to engage. If they’re growing up in child poverty, like so many do in my constituency, they may not have the money for travel, equipment, or the stability that they need to take up an opportunity, if that opportunity's there. And particularly in the Valleys, transport, as we know, can be a real barrier. You can have a college course, apprenticeship or job available, but if a young person can't get there reliably or affordably that opportunity is, effectively, out of reach for them.

And that's why this has to be a cross-Government issue. Education and skills are a big part of the answer, and having those spaces as well is so important. But so are mental health, tackling child poverty, transport, the economy, and support for young people and their families.

Not every young person is going to follow the same path. Some will go to university, some into apprenticeships, some straight into employment, and some might take a little longer to find their route as well, and all of those options are okay. But what matters is that they have the opportunity to find it. A young person growing up in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni should have the same chances to succeed as someone growing up anywhere else in Wales, because talent is spread equally across the whole of Wales, but opportunity isn't. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Gwnsler Cyffredinol. Many have called for youth justice to be devolved to Wales, including the Brown commission, and I'm glad that this Plaid Cymru Government also wants to see that happen. Currently, a child in the justice system in Wales has one foot in each world. Their school, healthcare and social workers are devolved, yet their court and their custody are not. That jagged edge means different systems, different governments, and it's the child who tends to slip through the gaps. contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Over the summer, I actually witnessed first-hand the devastation that wildfires caused across Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni. A wildfire actually broke out in my own village. When you see those flames outside of your window—. It's really difficult to understand the fear that they bring until you see it first-hand. You lie awake at night wondering whether, at any moment, you might have to actually leave your home because of how intense the fire gets. But thanks to the brilliant work of the fire and rescue service, the military, local communities, farmers and so many others, the fires were brought under control. contributions.item_title_en: 7. Reform UK Debate: A Welsh Rivers Act
contributions.text_english:
I welcome Reform UK's new-found interest in environmental protection, as it's not an issue you usually associate with this party. So, I genuinely hope that today marks a real and lasting commitment to the rivers, landscapes and ecosystems that define our communities, our economy and our way of life.

But I have to be honest, there is a deep contradiction at the heart of today's motion. You cannot stand in this Chamber and demand clean rivers while spending your political energy attacking the very environmental policies that protect them. You cannot claim to love Wales while dismissing the science that tells us what is happening to it.

People across Wales are angry, and they have every right to be. Six of the 20 most polluted rivers in the entire United Kingdom are here in Wales. Rivers that have been at the heart of our communities for generations are being poisoned. For too long, companies have taken the profits while our communities have been left to live with those consequences. People want accountability, they want action and they want the places they love handed on to the next generation in a better condition than they found them.

But you do not protect rivers by denying environmental realities everywhere else. You do not restore nature by attacking the policies designed to safeguard it. You do not become environmental champions simply because you have noticed that tackling water pollution is popular with voters.

This is a party that has consistently dismissed the science, ignored the evidence and undermined environmental policy at every opportunity. And that ignorance has consequences—real consequences—for real communities, because healthy rivers, restored wetlands and protected natural landscapes don't just look beautiful, they hold water back, they reduce flood risks and they protect people's homes. When you attack the environmental policies, you are not scoring political points, you are leaving communities—communities that you represent, that we all represent—more exposed, more vulnerable and more at risk. Welsh communities deserve better than that, and Plaid Cymru will do things differently.

We will protect our rivers, we will fight for the control of our water, we will reform regulatory oversight, strengthen the accountability of polluters, and drive real improvements in the environmental protection of our rivers, lakes and seas. If Reform is serious about our rivers, then be serious about the wider environmental emergency too, because the people of Wales deserve more than political opportunism dressed up as principle: they deserve sustained, credible, honest action. You don't get to spend years kicking down the door of environmental protection and then walk through the rubble claiming to be the ones who will rebuild it.
